tagline: Where minarets and church towers share the skyline
overview:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is a roughly heart-shaped country in the western Balkans, about the size of Costa Rica, wrapped by Croatia, Serbia, and Montenegro. Bosnia is the larger, mountainous northern part; Herzegovina is the sunnier southern region around the city of Mostar. The country touches the Adriatic Sea at just one spot, a 20-kilometer stretch of coast at the town of Neum. The capital, Sarajevo, lies in a long valley ringed by mountains that hosted the 1984 Winter Olympics.

About 3.3 million people live here, belonging mainly to three groups: Bosniaks, who are mostly Muslim; Serbs, mostly Orthodox Christian; and Croats, mostly Catholic. Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are all official languages and are so close that everyone understands one another. Because of a peace agreement that ended a war in 1995, the country has an unusually complex government, with two self-governing regions and a three-person presidency that rotates the top job. Life today centers on family, slow coffee, and rebuilt old towns.
landAndNature: The Dinaric Alps cover most of the country, rising to Maglić at 2,386 meters on the border with Montenegro. In Sutjeska National Park, the Perućica forest is one of the last primeval forests in Europe, where beech and fir trees have never been logged. Rivers are a special glory: the Neretva runs a startling emerald green through Herzegovina, the Una spills over wide travertine waterfalls, and the Drina slices through deep canyons. Karst limestone hides caves like Vjetrenica, home to blind cave creatures. Brown bears, wolves, and chamois live in the highlands, and Hutovo Blato wetlands shelter thousands of migrating birds. Inland winters are snowy; Herzegovina has hot, dry Mediterranean summers.
peopleAndCulture: Sarajevo is nicknamed the Jerusalem of Europe because a mosque, a Catholic cathedral, an Orthodox church, and a synagogue stand within a few minutes' walk of each other. Coffee is brewed thick in a long-handled copper pot called a džezva and sipped slowly with a sugar cube. The most loved food is ćevapi, small grilled minced-meat sausages tucked into soft somun bread with raw onion, followed by flaky burek pies and syrupy baklava. Sevdalinka, a soulful traditional song style, is often called the Bosnian blues. Every summer, divers leap 24 meters from Mostar's Old Bridge in a contest held since the 1500s. Soccer and basketball are the top sports, and the writer Ivo Andrić won the Nobel Prize for his novel The Bridge on the Drina.
history: A medieval Kingdom of Bosnia flourished before the Ottoman Empire conquered it in 1463; over four centuries of Ottoman rule, many Bosnians became Muslim, and mosques, bridges, and bazaars were built. Austria-Hungary took control in 1878. On June 28, 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne was shot in Sarajevo, an event that set off World War I. Bosnia then became part of Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia broke apart, Bosnia declared independence in 1992 and a terrible war followed among its peoples. About 100,000 people died, Sarajevo endured a siege of nearly four years, and in July 1995 around 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed at Srebrenica in what courts have ruled a genocide. The Dayton Agreement ended the fighting in late 1995, and the country became a candidate to join the European Union in 2022.
funFacts: Sarajevo tested one of Europe's first electric streetcar lines in 1885, before Vienna had one.
The Tunnel of Hope, dug under Sarajevo's airport during the siege, carried food, medicine, and people in and out of the city.
Mostar's Old Bridge was destroyed in 1993 and rebuilt stone by stone using original 16th-century methods, reopening in 2004.
Red resin fills some shell craters in Sarajevo's sidewalks; locals call these memorials Sarajevo roses.
Medieval tombstones called stećci, carved with dancers, hunters, and spirals, number about 60,000 across the region.
